idiom_name: MockK mockk<T>() + every { } returns/throws, coEvery for suspend
implementation_notes: MockK builds the double from a class or interface with mockk<Clock>() and the test configures answers through the every { ... } returns ... DSL (given as the BDD alias), with throws for failures and coEvery for suspending members, while relaxed mocks (@RelaxedMockK, relaxed = true) are the explicit opt-in when only some members matter; verification modes cover atLeast, atMost and exactly, and mocks are strict by default, so an unstubbed call fails instead of returning a default. That DSL is the configuration interface; MockK 1.13 and later support Kotlin 1.4 and higher, and it instruments final Kotlin classes, which is why it is preferred over Mockito on the JVM.
pitfalls: Inline functions, static members and object declarations need mockkStatic/mockkObject, which mutate global state for the whole JVM test run and must be unmocked afterwards.
Suspend members require coEvery/coVerify; mixing them with every silently fails to configure the call.
The default strictness means the fake must answer every call the SUT makes, so a missing stub appears as a test failure inside the SUT rather than at the configuration site.

variants.name: Hand-written fake with configurable properties
variants.idiom_name: reusable fake class with configurable vals and function properties
variants.implementation_notes: A hand-written fake implements the collaborator interface (which in Kotlin can also carry default implementations, so only the interesting members must be overridden) and exposes constructor parameters, settable vars or function-typed properties that the test configures; Kotlin's function types make this the same configurable-interface idea without a mocking library. Prefer it when the double should carry real behaviour such as an in-memory repository, when the class under test is final and instrumentation is unwanted, or when the test module must stay dependency-free.
pitfalls: Function-typed properties are mutable state; a fake declared as a field in a shared test fixture keeps the previous test's answers.
Properties in Kotlin interfaces cannot hold backing fields, so the fake must implement the accessor and cannot simply inherit configurable state from the interface.
Overriding a member that the interface provides with a default implementation silently changes behaviour for every test that uses the fake.
